title: When AI acts, the designer needs to design control
description: An AI that answers is different from an AI that acts. How to design autonomy levels, feedback, undo and trust when the system takes actions.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: AI agents that act inside the CRM and keep the person in control.

blocks.text: There's an important difference between an AI that answers and an AI that acts.

data.a2: Now the system has to do something.
data.maybe: And maybe even make decisions I didn't specify.
data.here: This is where the experience starts to change.
data.why: When AI goes from a tool that answers to a technology that acts, design has to think about something that doesn't always get much attention:

blocks.text: When the system does more, the user needs to understand more
In a traditional interface, we can follow most of the process.
With agents, we can just say what we want and wait.
That's convenient.
But it also raises a new question:
What is the system doing while I wait?
If we don't know, trust starts to drop.
That's why systems that act need to communicate enough for the person to keep a sense of what's going on.
“What did you understand?”
This may be one of the most important questions in an agent interface.
Imagine you say:
“Book a table for Saturday night.”
A lot of information might be missing.
What time?
For how many people?
At which restaurant?
The system can ask.
Or it can assume.
But the more it assumes, the higher the risk of getting it wrong.
A good experience needs to know when to act and when to ask for clarification.
Autonomy needs limits
Not every action carries the same risk.

blocks.caption: The bigger the impact of the action, the more control the interface needs to give before the AI acts.

blocks.text: We can think in different levels.
Low impact

items: Here, we can allow more autonomy

blocks.text: Medium impact
It may be important to show what will be done before it runs.
High impact
In this case, confirmation can matter a lot more.
Design needs to help define these limits.
“Automatic” doesn't mean “no interface”
There's an idea that agents will eliminate interfaces.
I'm not sure it's that simple.
Maybe they reduce the number of screens we have to navigate.
But that doesn't mean the interface disappears.
Its role may change.
Instead of being just a place to perform tasks, it can be a place to:
The interface can become a supervision layer.
Feedback changes too
In a traditional interface, we're used to states like:
But when an agent runs a complex task, that may not be enough.

data.lead: The system may need to show:
msgs: I picked Z because it fits your rules.
I need your confirmation before I continue.
data.a: That doesn't mean turning the interface into an endless list of messages.
data.b: It means giving enough visibility for the user to follow an action they aren't performing directly.

blocks.text: Errors matter even more
Every system makes mistakes.
But when an AI only answers, we can correct the answer.
When an AI performs an action, the mistake can have bigger consequences.
So we need to think ahead:
What happens if the agent misunderstands?
How does the user notice?
How do we undo the action?
Is there a history?
Can we stop the process?
Is there a manual alternative?
These questions are part of UX.
The “undo” button may become more important than ever
In systems with more autonomy, recovery mechanisms are essential.

blocks.caption: Trust isn't about hiding complexity: it's about showing what's going to happen.

blocks.text: If the agent did something wrong, we need clear paths to fix it.

data.a: These options shouldn't be treated as details.
data.b: They're part of trusting the system.

blocks.text: Trust doesn't mean hiding complexity
Sometimes we think a good AI experience is one where everything happens automatically and the user doesn't even notice.
But there's a limit.
If the system does important things without explaining anything, the experience can feel comfortable at first and scary later.
The user needs to know enough to trust it.
That doesn't mean showing all the inner workings of the AI.
It means explaining what matters for the decision.
What was understood.
What will be done.
What has already happened.
What needs approval.
What can be changed.
The designer starts designing behavior
In a traditional interface, we design states.
In an agent experience, we also need to design behaviors.
For example:
If the user asks for something ambiguous → ask.
If it's a high-impact action → ask for confirmation.
If there isn't enough information → explain what's missing.
If the system isn't confident enough → don't make things up.
If the action fails → explain and offer an alternative.
This feels much closer to designing product rules than just designing screens.
And that's exactly why UX still matters.
AI can execute. The designer needs to define how it should behave.
The more capability we give the system, the more we need to think about the rules.
What can it do?
What can't it do?
When should it ask?
When should it act?
When should it stop?
When should it ask for help?
How should it explain?
How does the user take back control?
These questions are a big part of the experience.
In the end, autonomy and control need to go together
I don't think the goal of a good AI experience is to give as much autonomy as possible.
The goal is to find the level of autonomy that makes sense for each situation.
For some tasks, we want the AI to do everything.

items: For others, we want to follow along
For others, we want to decide every step
Good design doesn't force a single model

blocks.text: Maybe the new UX question is a different one
For a long time we asked:
“How do we get the user to complete this task?”
With agents, maybe we need to ask:
“How much of this task should the system do on its own?”
It seems like a small shift.
But it completely changes how we think about digital products.
Because when the system starts acting, UX isn't only about making actions easier.
It's also about setting limits, building trust and keeping people in control.
